212.stem: There are two tanks on a property, Tank $A$ and Tank $B$. Initially, Tank $A$ holds 1000 litres of water and Tank $B$ is empty.

parts.latex:
Tank $B$ remains empty until $t=15$ when water is added to it at a constant rate of 30 litres per minute.

By drawing a line on the grid on the previous page, or otherwise, find the value of $t$ when the two tanks contain the same volume of water.
can_use: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

Simultaneous equations.reason: Assumed-algebra skill used only as an optional algebraic check of the graph reading.

Piecewise-defined functions.reason: Only the t>=15 linear piece is used to find the intersection; the piecewise rule itself is not needed.

Equations of straight lines.evidence: Tank B: V=30(t-15) for t>=15 ... drawn on the grid
Equations of straight lines.reason: Writing and graphing the Tank B line earns the first mark.

parts.latex: Using the graphs drawn, or otherwise, find the value of $t$ (where $t>0$) when the total volume of water in the two tanks is 1000 litres.
can_use: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

solutions.latex: \exfigure{33_q11_1}

Tank $B$: $V=30(t-15)$ for $t\ge15$. This line starts at $(15,0)$ and rises $30$ litres each minute; drawn on the grid in part (a), it meets the Tank $A$ line at $t=29$.

\exfigure{33_q11_1}

Check algebraically:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000-20t &= 30(t-15)\\ 1000-20t &= 30t-450\\ 1450 &= 50t\\ t &= 29 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The tanks hold the same volume after $29$ minutes.
criteria: Draws the graph of volume for tank $B$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $t\ge15$, the total volume is
$$\begin{aligned} (1000-20t)+30(t-15) &= 1000\\ 10t-450 &= 0\\ t &= 45 \end{aligned}$$
(For $0<t<15$ the total is $1000-20t<1000$.) Tank $A$ is not yet empty at $t=45$ ($V=100$), so the model still applies.

$\therefore$ $t=45$ minutes.

parts.latex:
Katrina runs a business refurbishing old computers.

The cost, $C$ dollars, of refurbishing $n$ computers is given by $C=3n^2+100$.

The income, $I$ dollars, received from selling $n$ computers is given by $I=80n$.

Determine the minimum and maximum number of computers that Katrina can refurbish and sell to make a profit.

solutions.latex:
Solve $3n^2+100=80n$.

$$\begin{aligned}3n^2-80n+100&=0\\ n&=\dfrac{80\pm\sqrt{(-80)^2-4\times 3\times 100}}{2\times 3}\\ n&=1.315,\ 25.352\end{aligned}$$

Katrina will make a profit when $I>C$ and this occurs for $2\le n\le 25$, where $n$ represents the number of computers refurbished and sold.

Hence, the minimum number is 2 and the maximum number is 25 in order to make a profit.
criteria: Solves quadratic equation and finds two non-integer solutions for $n$
Forms quadratic equation to find break-even points, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
An object is thrown vertically upwards from the top of a tall building. The height, $h$ metres, of the object above the ground after $t$ seconds is given by

$$h=45+12t-2t^2.$$

The object reaches its maximum height 3 seconds after it is thrown. The diagram shows the graph of $h(t)$ for $t\ge 0$.

\exfigure{1632_q5_1}

What is the vertical distance, in metres, that the object rises above the top of the building?

solutions.latex:
The top of the building is the height at $t=0$:
$$h(0)=45$$
The maximum height occurs at $t=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} h(3)&=45+12(3)-2(3)^2\\ &=63 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the object rises $63-45=18$ m above the top of the building.

638.stem: Eric is organising a gala dinner. The function centre will charge him \$2 000 to hire the room and he needs to pay a catering company \$80 per person for food.

figures.cap: income and cost lines C against n

parts.latex: Write an equation for the cost \$$C$ of hosting the event for $n$ people.
What is the profit if 75 people attend the dinner?

solutions.latex:
The cost is $\$2000$ for the room plus $\$80$ for each of the $n$ people:
$$C=80n+2000$$

From the graph, the income and cost lines intersect at $n=50$ (and $C=\$6000$).

$\therefore$ 50 people are required to break even.

From the graph, when 75 people attend, the income is $\$9000$ and the costs are $\$8000$:
$$9000-8000=1000$$
$\therefore$ The profit is $\$1000$ when 75 people attend.

1044.stem:
Jayme has \$100. He starts to save \$25 each week to buy a new racing bike.

His savings can be modelled by $S=100+25t$, where $S$ is the dollars saved and $t$ is the time in weeks from when he started saving the money.

figures.cap: blank grid: S from 0 to 2000 (gridlines every 100), t from 0 to 50 weeks
solution sketch: grid with Jayme: S1 = 100 + 25t and Jorge: S2 = 40(t - 8) lines; dashed lines at t = 28 (intersection) and t = 48 (gap of $300)

parts.latex:
On the grid below, draw the graph of this model and label it as Jayme's savings.

\exfigure{1372_q11_1}

Jorge, Jayme's brother, wanted to start saving 8 weeks after Jayme began saving. He initially had no money but saves \$40 each week.

By drawing a line on the grid above, or otherwise, find the value of $t$ when the two brothers have the same money.
can_use: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

parts.latex: Using the graph, or otherwise, find the value of $t$ when Jorge's savings is \$300 more than Jayme's savings.

meta.top_criterion_original: Correct graph of $S_1=100+25t$, labelled as Jayme's savings
meta.marker_note: The graph of $S_1=100+25t$ must be labelled as Jayme's savings.

solutions.latex:
Reading from the graph, the lines intersect at $t=28$ weeks.

Or: Jorge's savings are $S_2=40(t-8)$ for $t\ge8$. Equating the savings:
$$\begin{aligned}40(t-8)&=100+25t\\40t-320&=100+25t\\15t&=420\\t&=28\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore t=28\text{ weeks}$$
criteria: Forms the equation $40(t-8)=100+25t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Reading from the graph, the gap is \$300 at $t=48$ weeks.

Or:
$$\begin{aligned}40(t-8)-(100+25t)&=300\\40t-320-100-25t&=300\\15t-420&=300\\15t&=720\\t&=48\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore t=48\text{ weeks}$$

1329.stem: 25 students sit an exam with a total mark out of 40. For each of the 25 students, the number $x$ of the lessons missed and the number $y$ of the marks lost on the test were recorded. The total number of marks lost was 230 more than the total number of lessons missed. The correlation coefficient between lessons missed and marks lost was $r=0.81$ and the least squares regression line of marks lost on lessons missed has equation $y=1.5x+6$.

parts.latex: Describe the nature and strength of the correlation between lessons missed and marks lost.
parts.note: Describing correlation: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S1-06 / MST-12-S2-08

parts.latex: Given that the least squares regression line of marks lost on lessons missed passes through the point $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$, find the mean number of lessons missed and marks lost.
Find the equation of the least squares regression line of marks gained on lessons missed.
parts.note: Regression line of a transformed response: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S1-06 / MST-12-S2-08

solutions.latex: Strong, positive, linear relationship

$y=1.5x+6$

Total marks lost $=25\bar{y}$

Total lessons missed $=25\bar{x}$

The total marks lost is 230 more than the total lessons missed:
$$25\bar{x}+230=25\bar{y}\quad(1)$$
The line passes through $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$:
$$\bar{y}=1.5\bar{x}+6\quad(2)$$
Substituting (2) into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}25\bar{x}+230&=25(1.5\bar{x}+6)\\ 25\bar{x}+230&=37.5\bar{x}+150\\ 80&=12.5\bar{x}\\ \bar{x}&=6.4\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\bar{y}&=1.5(6.4)+6\\ &=15.6\end{aligned}$$

Since the test is out of 40, marks gained $=40-y$.

$\therefore$ least squares regression line for marks gained on lessons missed:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Marks gained}&=40-(1.5x+6)\\ &=40-6-1.5x\\ &=-1.5x+34\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Break-even occurs where $R=C$.

From the graph, the two lines intersect at $x=20$.

Algebraically:

$$\begin{aligned} R &= C \\ 1000+20x &= 1200+10x \\ 10x &= 200 \\ x &= 20 \end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 mark (no marking criteria shown in source)

solutions.latex:
Profit is revenue minus cost, so a profit of $\$500$ needs $R-C=500$.

$$\begin{aligned} R-C &= 500 \\ 1000+20x-(1200+10x) &= 500 \\ 10x &= 700 \\ x &= 70 \end{aligned}$$

1649.stem: The population of a town in NSW has shown a linear decline in the years 2011 to 2019. In 2011 the population was 34300 people. In 2019 it was 27740 people.

parts.latex: Write a linear equation expressing the population of the town, $P$, as a function of $t$, the number of years since 2011.
If the town is still experiencing a linear decline, what will the population be in 2025?

solutions.latex:
The population is linear, so $P=34300+kt$.

In 2019, $t=8$ and $P=27740$:
$$\begin{aligned} 27740&=34300+8k \\ k&=-820 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore P=-820t+34300$$
criteria: Correct working finding the declining rate, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In 2025, $t=14$:
$$\begin{aligned} P&=-820\times14+34300 \\ &=22\,820 \text{ people} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: The formula for the cost involved in selling $N$ Midiens in a day is $C=10N+300$. What is the cost when 20 Midiens are sold in a day?
Draw the line representing the equation $C=10N+300$ on the graph on page 12.
How many Midiens would they need to sell in a day to break even?
can_use: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

parts.latex: How much profit or loss would they make on a day where they sold 30 Midiens? Clearly state profit or loss.

solutions.latex:
Substituting $N=20$ into $C=10N+300$:
$$\begin{aligned} C &= 10\times 20+300 \\ &= 500 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the cost is } \$500$$

The line $C=10N+300$ has $C$-intercept $300$ (fixed costs), and from part (a) passes through $(20,\,500)$. A second point is $N=40$, $C=700$.

\exfigure{394_q14_s1}
criteria: Plots one correct point, or draws a line with the correct gradient, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Break-even occurs where income equals cost, $I=C$.
$$\begin{aligned} 30N &= 10N+300 \\ 20N &= 300 \\ N &= 15 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{they must sell 15 Midiens}$$

When $N=30$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{income} &= 30\times 30 = \$900 \\ \text{cost} &= 10\times 30+300 = \$600 \\ \text{profit} &= 900-600 = \$300 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{a profit of } \$300$$

1974.stem: Jamie owns a company producing and selling pizzas. The income function of $y=20x$ is shown on the graph below, where $x$ is the number of pizzas sold. The cost of producing these pizzas includes a set up cost of \$50 and additional costs of \$2 per pizza.

figures.cap: grid with income line y=20x from the origin, y axis to 150 and x axis to 14
solution sketch: cost line y=2x+50 drawn on the grid with the income line

parts.latex: Write the cost function in the form $y=mx+c$

Sketch the cost function on the axis below:

\exfigure{416_q13_1}
Hence, determine Jamie's break even point.
can_use: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

solutions.latex:
The cost is the set-up cost plus $\$2$ for each of the $x$ pizzas:
$$y=2x+50$$

\exfigure{416_q13_s1}

The cost function $y=2x+50$ is a straight line with $y$-intercept $50$ and gradient $2$.
criteria: Draws a straight line with the correct $y$-intercept or gradient, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Break even is where income equals cost:
$$\begin{aligned}20x&=2x+50\\ 18x&=50\\ x&=\dfrac{25}{9}\approx2.78\end{aligned}$$
At this point $y=20\cdot\dfrac{25}{9}=\dfrac{500}{9}\approx55.56$. Pizzas are sold whole: for $2$ pizzas the income is $\$40$ and the cost $\$54$, and for $3$ pizzas the income is $\$60$ and the cost $\$56$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Jamie must sell }3\text{ pizzas to break even}$$

meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the break-even value was $2.83$ pizzas; $50\div18=2.78$. The whole-number answer, $3$ pizzas, is unchanged.
meta.format_note: Source gives only the number of pizzas; the break-even point $\left(\frac{25}{9},\frac{500}{9}\right)$ is added. The question asks for the point, so the owner may want the coordinates as the marked answer.
